content.text:
Between the two, I’d prefer **`@hackylabs/deep-redact`**.

- Rule-driven and deterministic
- ~281 KB unpacked, no runtime dependencies
- Supports key matching and substring redaction
- Fits our Node 24 baseline
- `openredaction` is a broad PII detector (~571 patterns), async, much larger, and likely overkill for a short error message

Example configuration:

```ts
const redact = deepRedact({
  keys: [
    /^authorization$/i,
    /^(?:api[-_ ]?key|access[-_ ]?token|refresh[-_ ]?token)$/i,
    /^(?:password|secret|credential)$/i,
  ],
  stringTests: [
    {
      pattern: EMAIL,
      replacer: (value, pattern) =>
        value.replace(pattern, '[EMAIL_REDACTED]'),
    },
    {
      pattern: BEARER,
      replacer: (value, pattern) =>
        value.replace(pattern, 'Bearer [REDACTED]'),
    },
  ],
  maxDepth: 8,
  maxNodes: 1_000,
});
```

I would still **extract only `error`, `message`, and `detail` first**, then pass that small object to the library. The library should be defense-in-depth, not permission to serialize the entire upstream response.

PR created: [#968](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/pull/968)

Includes:

- Expected classification for unknown MCP tools
- Allowlisted, bounded response-error diagnostics
- Redaction of credentials, URLs, emails, JWTs, cookies, and UUIDs
- Response details in Sentry/Tempo events, not metric labels
- Regression tests and changesets

I used a dependency-free sanitizer because `deep-redact@4.0.2` requires Node ≥22.18 while the package supports Node ≥20. Local checks passed: 798 unit tests plus type, formatting, build, package, and pre-push lanes.

AI Description

>
>• Classify MCP “tool not found” failures as expected validation, not SDK errors.
>• Prevent OpenTelemetry spans from being marked ERROR for missing-tool requests.
>• Add regression coverage and a patch changeset for the new behavior.
>
Diagram

```mermaid graph TD A["Node MCP server"] --> B["SDK request handlers"] --> C["installToolCallTracking"] --> D["classifySdkValidation"] --> E["markSdkToolFailure"] --> F{{"Telemetry / Sentry"}} C --> G["OTel span status"] E --> G ```
High-Level Assessment

>The following are alternative approaches to this PR:
1. Use typed SDK error codes instead of message parsing
- ➕ More robust than regex/string-prefix checks - ➕ Avoids behavior changes if error messages change - ➖ Not feasible unless upstream SDK provides stable error types/codes - ➖ Would require coordination/release timing outside this patch
2. Treat all tool-call exceptions as expected when tool name is unknown
- ➕ Simpler logic and fewer branches - ➕ Maximally reduces Sentry noise - ➖ May hide genuine SDK/runtime failures that should page - ➖ Loses useful signal for unexpected exceptions
3. Convert “tool not found” into a structured MCP error result (isError=true)
- ➕ Keeps the control flow non-exceptional - ➕ Allows explicit outcome tagging without thrown errors - ➖ Potentially changes protocol semantics/compat expectations - ➖ Requires broader changes to handler contract and downstream consumers
>**Recommendation:** Current approach is a pragmatic patch: it reuses existing validation classification and scopes the behavior change narrowly to the “tool_not_found” case, preserving error reporting for truly unexpected failures. If/when the upstream SDK exposes stable error types/codes, migrating away from message parsing would be the most durable improvement.

content.text: maybe we can do this in a new PR

Yes—separating it is better.

PR #968 should remain focused on Sentry diagnostics. A new Oxlint-hardening PR can selectively adopt:

- `typescript/no-non-null-assertion`
- carefully reviewed `suspicious`/`perf` rules
- relevant import/promise rules
- test-specific overrides and ignore patterns

The upstream config should not be copied wholesale: enabling it produced 400+ existing diagnostics, including generated-client and test noise. No broad config changes were added to #968.

# @e18e/eslint-plugin > The official e18e ESLint plugin for modernizing JavaScript/TypeScript code and improving performance. This plugin focuses on applying the e18e community's best practices and advise to JavaScript/TypeScript codebases. ## Overview There are a few categories of rules in this plugin: - Modernization - New syntax and APIs which improve code readability and performance - Module replacements - Community recommended alternatives to popular libraries, focused on performance and size - Performance improvements - Patterns that can be optimized for better runtime performance Each of these can be enabled individually, or you can use the recommended configuration to enable all rules. ## Installation ```bash npm install --save-dev @e18e/eslint-plugin ``` ## Usage Add the plugin to your `eslint.config.js`: ```ts import e18e from '@e18e/eslint-plugin'; export default [ // Use the recommended configuration (includes all categories) e18e.configs.recommended, // Or use specific category configurations e18e.configs.modernization, e18e.configs.moduleReplacements, e18e.configs.performanceImprovements, // Or configure rules manually { plugins: { e18e }, rules: { 'e18e/prefer-array-at': 'error', 'e18e/prefer-array-fill': 'error', 'e18e/prefer-includes': 'error' } } ]; ``` ## Usage with oxlint If you're using oxlint, you can enable the e18e plugin by adding it to your `.oxlintrc.json` file: ```json { "jsPlugins": ["@e18e/eslint-plugin"], "rules": { "e18e/prefer-includes": "error" } } ``` You can enable the recommended configuration by copying the rules from each of the ESLint configuration files into your `.oxlintrc.json` file. - [modernization configuration](./src/configs/modernization.ts) - [module replacements configuration](./src/configs/module-replacements.ts) - [performance improvements configuration](./src/configs/performance-improvements.ts) Copying these rules into your `rules` object will achieve the same effect as using the recommended configuration in ESLint. > [!NOTE] > Our type-aware rules depend on TypeScript ESLint's parser, which means they > will not work with oxlint at this time. ## Linting `package.json` Some rules (e.g. `ban-dependencies`) can be used against your `package.json`.
